segments.say: Every project has a rule that everybody agrees with and everybody eventually breaks. On this one it is in the brief, in plain words: no personal data, and no emojis. Now, you could put that in the memory file and hope. Or you could make the machine check it every single time a file is written... which is what a hook is. Not a suggestion in a document. A thing that fires. But first I asked which rule is easiest to break by accident, and it picked neither of mine. It picked the deterministic seed. An emoji or a name shows up in the diff. Determinism fails silently — you find out when seed forty-two replays differently. And think about why the memory file is not enough on its own. It is advice. It competes for attention with everything else in the window, it gets summarised when things get long, and on a bad afternoon it simply loses. A hook does not compete with anything. It is not persuasion. It is plumbing. And there is a reason this is the third thing we build and not the first. A hook is only worth writing once you know what the rule is. Spend a week guessing and you automate the wrong thing — and an automated wrong thing is much harder to argue with than a note in a document.

So it writes the check, and then it does something better than writing the check: it shows me the cases. Look at what I asked for, though, because the second half of the request is the part that matters: write the check as a small script in the repo so I can read it. Not a rule buried in a settings file. A file I can open. And it builds them in the right order: the checker first, wired up only once it is proven. Then a small piece of honesty on the way through. It thinks the binary-file guard came out as a literal space, which would have made the checker exit clean on almost every file — and a rule that passes everything looks exactly like a rule that works. Then it corrects itself again: it is a real null byte, the guard is fine, but it makes the script read as binary to grep. So it replaces it with an escape. Then the wiring itself, seventeen lines of settings. PostToolUse, matched against edit, write, multi-edit and notebook-edit, with a fifteen second timeout, pulling the edited file path off the payload the harness hands it. And it tests the hook the way the harness will call it — piping the real payload in, rather than running the script by hand. One of those tests kills its own shell, and it works out why before blaming the hook: the test ran exit zero in-process, and the hook gets a shell of its own. A test artefact, named as one. A line with a region name, a driver id and a destination — passes. A comment with a tick emoji — blocked. A driver field with a person's name in it — blocked. An email address — blocked. A copyright symbol — passes. And read why that last one passes, because it is the whole difficulty in miniature. Emoji detection is exact; it is a property of the character. Detecting a real person's name is not something a script can do reliably. Leeds is capitalised. South East is capitalised. Control Tower is capitalised. Morgan is both a person and a place. So rather than pretend, it narrows the job to the two shapes a leak actually takes in this repository: an email address, and a person-ish field — driver, customer, contact, recipient — holding a capitalised value. And then the line I would put on a poster. It deliberately did not write a deny-list of real names to check against... because that file would itself be a list of real names, committed to the repository. The thing the rule exists to prevent. And one consequence it flags that is easy to miss: this hook applies to the simulator agent still building in the background. It is held to the same rule as I am, which is what you want — but if the check fires a false positive in there, what you see is a blocked write inside a report you were not reading closely. One more thing it noticed while we were not looking. The settings file was picked up without a restart, even though the specialist we wrote earlier still is not. So those two are loaded by different mechanisms, and the problem we hit last lecture is narrower than nothing in this folder reloads. Now think about what that choice actually buys. A check that is right most of the time and wrong occasionally is worse than useless, because you stop reading its output. The moment you are overriding a rule twice a day, you have trained yourself to override it. So it narrowed the rule until it could be enforced honestly, and told me plainly where the edges are. That is the difference between a check you keep and a check you delete in a fortnight. And there is a design decision underneath all of this that is worth saying out loud. The rule came from the brief. I wrote one line about personal data and emojis in a document, days ago, and it has now become a script that runs on every edit, in every session, for anybody who clones this repository. That is the shape of everything we are doing this week: you say what good looks like, once, carefully... and then you spend your effort making it fire by itself rather than repeating it. Watch how it tests, too, because this is the habit worth stealing. It did not write the checker and declare it done. It built a table of cases first — the ones that must pass, the ones that must fail, and the ones it should refuse to judge at all — and then showed me that table rather than the code. That is the right level to review at. I do not want to read a regular expression. I want to know what it lets through. And notice the third column, the one marked skipped: the checker itself, missing files, binaries, lockfiles. Deciding what a rule should ignore is as much of the design as deciding what it catches. A check that fires on a lock file is a check somebody disables on a Friday afternoon. One more thing about where this lives. It is in the project settings, which means it travels with the repository. Anybody who clones this gets the rule, whether or not they read the brief, whether or not they were in this conversation. That is what it means to encode a standard rather than announce one.

Now break it on purpose. One line, with a lorry emoji in it. Blocked. It names the file, the line, the exact codepoint, and then it repeats the rule back at me. And read the last line, because it is not a complaint: fix the line and write the file again. That is the difference between a check that stops work and one that redirects it. The turn can recover without me. And notice how specific the complaint is. Not the file breaks a rule. The file, the line number, the exact codepoint, and the rule in the words I wrote it in. That is what makes an automated check something a person will actually act on rather than route around.

Be precise about what just happened. This hook runs after the write, so the file did land on disk. What the hook does is exit with an error, which stops the turn carrying on as if nothing was wrong. It is a tripwire, not a lock on the door. If you want the door locked, that is a different event — a pre-tool hook, reading the content before it reaches disk. Fiddlier, and it exists.

Which brings us to the last part. That was one event, after one kind of tool. There are others: before a tool runs, when a session starts, when the agent is about to hand back to you. And the useful mental shift is this. You have spent two lectures teaching an agent what you want by writing it down. A hook is the first thing today that does not ask the agent to remember anything at all. It just happens. When a rule genuinely matters, stop writing it in a document that has to be read... and put it somewhere that fires whether anyone read it or not. And one detail from earlier is worth repeating, because it will save you an afternoon. The settings file was picked up without a restart. The specialist we wrote in the last lecture still was not. Same folder, different loading rules. So when something you added is not taking effect, the honest first question is not what did I get wrong — it is whether this particular thing is read once at startup, or every time. And one fires when you press enter — which is the example it picks, slipping a line of live simulator state into every message. Seed forty-two, tick eighteen thirty, eighty-seven point four percent on time. And notice we still have not written a line of the application ourselves. What we have built is the conditions the work happens in.
